Stop asking Google. Start asking science.

You know the loop: you type a health or nutrition question into Google, and what comes back is either SEO blogspam, a wellness influencer's confident guess, or a paywalled abstract you can't actually read past the first line. You never find out what the actual research says.

Consensus is an AI search engine built only on peer-reviewed research — over 200 million papers, pulled from Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, and its own crawl. Ask it something like "does magnesium help with sleep" or "is remote work actually less productive," and it gives you a Consensus Meter: a simple bar showing how many real studies say yes, no, possibly, or mixed. No ten open tabs. No guessing who's credible.

For bigger questions, Pro Search goes further — a synthesis of the findings, a timeline of how the research has developed, the leading authors in the field, and a map of what hasn't been studied enough yet. It even breaks specific claims down into evidence strength, so you can see not just what's said but how solid it is.

It's not perfect — the meter counts how papers lean, it doesn't quality-weight them like a real meta-analysis would, and the free plan's monthly searches disappear fast. But for the daily "wait, is that actually true" itch, it's a different category of tool than search.

Save this before you forget the name. Then next time you catch yourself about to argue about a health claim from a comments section, try Consensus instead — link in bio.
